seo_title: Trademark Opposition in India: Filing and Timeline
title: How to Oppose a Trademark Application in India: Procedure and Timelines
meta_description: How to oppose a trademark in India under Section 21: the four-month deadline, counter-statement and evidence stages, and what a missed deadline costs.
format: step-by-step process with timelines and fees where official
intro: Anyone can oppose a trademark application in India once it has been advertised in the Trade Marks Journal, and the opposition does not have to come from a competitor; a consumer body, an individual, or a company with no prior registration can all file one. The right question for a business that has just discovered a conflicting mark in the journal is not whether it can oppose but whether it can do so inside the four-month window, because that deadline is treated as close to absolute.

This guide sets out the stages of an opposition under Section 21 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 and the Trade Marks Rules, 2017, from the notice of opposition to the hearing, and flags the two points where applicants most often lose a mark they could otherwise have kept: missing the counter-statement deadline, and failing to file evidence on time.

sections.heading: Who can oppose, and on what grounds
paragraphs: Section 21(1) allows any person to give notice of opposition in writing within four months of the date the application was advertised or re-advertised in the Trade Marks Journal. The Registrar has no general discretion to accept a notice filed after that period; one Madras High Court matter records an opponent who tried to rely on COVID-19 disruption to justify a late filing and was still held to the limitation. An earlier regime under the 2002 Rules allowed an opponent to file within three months and ask for a further month, but the 2017 Rules removed that extension route, so the working assumption today should be that four months is the outer limit with no application for condonation available.

Grounds of opposition typically fall into a few recurring categories: that the mark is identical or deceptively similar to an earlier registered or well-known mark, that it is descriptive or generic for the goods or services claimed, that it was applied for in bad faith, or that it is scandalous, likely to deceive, or disentitled to protection under the general prohibitions in Sections 9 and 11 of the Act. An opposition built on a registered mark with an earlier filing date is almost always stronger than one resting only on unregistered use, though prior use that predates the applicant's filing can still defeat the application under the proviso to Section 11 if it is properly evidenced.
The notice of opposition is filed as Form TM-O before the Trade Marks Registry having jurisdiction over the application, with the prescribed fee, and must be served on the applicant by the Registry.

sections.heading: The counter-statement: a trap for the unwary applicant
paragraphs: Once the Registry serves the notice of opposition, the applicant has two months under Section 21(2) and Rule 44 to file a counter-statement setting out the facts relied on to support the application. This period is calculated from the date the applicant actually receives the copy of the notice, not from the date the opposition was filed. If the applicant does not file a counter-statement within the two months, the application is treated as abandoned, and the Registry closes the file without any further hearing.

This is the single most common way a legitimate trademark application is lost, usually because the counter-statement deadline was missed by an applicant who had changed addresses, switched trademark agents, or simply did not track the Registry correspondence closely enough. Because there is no condonation mechanism built into Section 21 for this step either, an applicant who realises late that the deadline has passed generally has to file a fresh application rather than revive the abandoned one.
Where the counter-statement is filed on time, the Registry serves a copy on the opponent, and the matter moves into the evidence stage.

sections.heading: Evidence stage: three rounds, one month each after the first two
paragraphs: Rules 45 to 47 of the 2017 Rules set out the evidence sequence. The opponent files evidence in support of the opposition, typically within two months of receiving the counter-statement, though the opponent may instead choose to rely on the facts stated in the notice of opposition without filing further evidence. The applicant then files evidence in support of the application, and the opponent has a further window to file evidence strictly in reply, limited to matters arising from the applicant's evidence rather than a fresh case.

Evidence is filed by affidavit, with documents such as sales figures, advertising spend, invoices, registration certificates from other jurisdictions, search reports, and correspondence annexed as exhibits. A mark that has been used extensively and continuously in India before the rival application was filed stands a materially better chance at this stage than one supported only by an assertion of reputation.

The Registry has shown some flexibility on extending these evidence timelines on a reasoned application, which is a different thing from extending the four-month opposition window itself or the two-month counter-statement window, both of which the Rules and the decided cases treat far more strictly.

sections.heading: The hearing and the Registrar's order
paragraphs: Once the evidence stage closes, either party may request a hearing before the Registrar, who considers the pleadings, the evidence, and the submissions before passing a reasoned order either refusing the application, allowing it to proceed to registration, or allowing it subject to conditions, amendments, or disclaimers. Decisions often turn on the comparison of the marks as a whole, the similarity of the goods or services, the nature of the likely consumer, and any evidence of actual confusion in the market.

An order of the Registrar in opposition proceedings is appealable. Since the dissolution of the Intellectual Property Appellate Board in 2021, appeals from Trade Marks Registry orders lie to the jurisdictional High Court, and several High Courts, including Delhi, Madras, and Calcutta, have set up specialised intellectual property divisions to hear them.

Parties sometimes settle an opposition mid-stream through a coexistence agreement, a change in the specification of goods, or withdrawal of the application in exchange for commercial terms. A settled opposition is usually resolved faster and more cheaply than a contested hearing, and the Registry will record a withdrawal or settlement without needing to decide the merits.

sections.heading: Before you oppose: practical checks
paragraphs: Confirm the advertisement date in the Trade Marks Journal before doing anything else, since the four-month clock runs from that date and re-advertisement after an amendment restarts it. Trawling through the weekly Journal, or subscribing to a watch service that flags conflicting filings as they are advertised, is the only reliable way to catch an opposition deadline before it closes; the Registry does not notify a trademark owner that a similar mark has been filed.

Weigh the opposition against a rectification petition. If the four-month window has already closed and the mark proceeds to registration, a cancellation petition under Section 47 or Section 57 of the Act remains available on broader grounds and without the same rigid time limit, though it is a slower and generally costlier route than an opposition filed in time.

Keep evidence of use current. A business planning to oppose, or expecting to be opposed, should maintain dated records of first use, continuous use, and the scale of its business under the mark well before any dispute arises, because affidavits filed years after the relevant facts carry noticeably less weight with the Registry than contemporaneous records.

faqs.q: Can I oppose a trademark after the four-month deadline has passed?
faqs.a: Generally no. The 2017 Rules removed the one-month extension that existed under the earlier regime, and courts have refused to condone delay even where the opponent cites disruptions such as the pandemic. Once the window closes, a cancellation petition after registration is the remaining option.

faqs.q: What happens if the applicant does not file a counter-statement?
faqs.a: The application is treated as abandoned under Section 21(2) if the counter-statement is not filed within two months of receiving the opposition notice. The Registry closes the file, and the applicant would normally need to file a fresh application rather than revive the abandoned one.

faqs.q: Does an opponent need a registered trademark to oppose?
faqs.a: No. Anyone can file an opposition, including on the basis of prior unregistered use, descriptiveness, bad faith, or likely deception. A registered mark with an earlier filing date is stronger evidence, but it is not a precondition to opposing.

faqs.q: Where does an appeal from the Registrar's opposition order go?
faqs.a: To the jurisdictional High Court. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board, which used to hear these appeals, was abolished in 2021, and several High Courts now run dedicated intellectual property divisions for this kind of appeal.
